title: Delhi High Court Refuses to Halt India's HPV Vaccination Drive, Seeks Centre's Response on Safety Concerns
excerpt: The court declined a stay on the national immunisation programme but called the issue 'very important' and ordered responses from ICMR, CDSCO, and NITAG.
body:
• The Delhi High Court refused to stay India's HPV vaccination drive after the Centre assured the vaccines are safe and administered only through government channels
  • A PIL challenged the rollout of Gardasil for 14-year-old girls, alleging insufficient long-term safety data and lack of informed parental consent
  • The court ordered responses from the Centre, ICMR, CDSCO, and NITAG, calling it a "very important issue" that requires a "cautious path"
  • Petitioners cited alleged severe neurological complications in a 14-year-old Tamil Nadu girl who received the vaccine in March 2026

Court Lets Vaccination Continue — For Now

The Delhi High Court on Wednesday declined to halt India's nationwide HPV vaccination campaign, ruling that there was "no reason why the administration of the vaccine should be stopped" after the Central government assured the court that the programme is being conducted safely through official channels.

A division bench comprising Chief Justice DK Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia was hearing a public interest litigation filed by gynaecologist Dr Sujata Mittal and fitness influencer Jitendra Chauksey. The petitioners challenged the inclusion of Gardasil, a quadrivalent HPV vaccine, in India's Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP), which targets 14-year-old girls through schools and public health systems.

While refusing the stay, the bench struck a cautious tone. "We are not doubting the government's intention, but the issue concerns all girl children and we have to tread a very cautious path," the court said, according to Bar and Bench.

Safety Concerns at the Heart of the Challenge

The petitioners argued that India's nationwide rollout — which began on February 28, 2026 — was implemented without conclusive long-term safety studies or adequate informed parental consent. They cited the case of a 14-year-old girl from Tamil Nadu who allegedly developed severe neurological complications, including paralysis-like weakness, loss of voice, and impaired vision, days after receiving the vaccine in March 2026.

Similar incidents were reported in Gwalior and Bihar, according to the petition. The PIL argued that frontline health workers, including ASHA workers, are given enrolment targets that create "undue pressure" on young girls to receive the vaccine.

"Half-baked vaccines should not be administered."

— Delhi High Court bench, addressing the Central government

Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, representing the Centre, told the bench that the vaccines are administered exclusively through government systems with appropriate safety measures in place.

What the Science Says

HPV — human papillomavirus — is the leading cause of cervical cancer, which remains one of the most common cancers among Indian women. The World Health Organisation recommends HPV vaccination for girls aged 9-14 as the most effective prevention strategy, and over 140 countries have included HPV vaccines in their national immunisation programmes.

India's rollout of Gardasil follows years of debate. The vaccine's history in the country is fraught — a 2013 Parliamentary Standing Committee report raised concerns about HPV vaccine trials conducted in Andhra Pradesh and Gujarat by PATH, citing procedural lapses around informed consent and monitoring.

What Happens Next

The court directed the Central government, ICMR, Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), and the National Immunization Technical Advisory Group (NITAG) to file responses to the PIL. The case will be heard next in the coming weeks.

For Indian families abroad, the case is worth watching. HPV vaccination is already standard in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia. India's rollout — if sustained — would represent a major public health step. But the court's decision to seek detailed government responses signals that questions about consent protocols and post-vaccination monitoring are being taken seriously.
nri_angle: HPV vaccination is standard in Western countries where most NRIs live; India's rollout and safety debate directly affects families with children in India.
